One day after the New Fourth Army Incident, Zhongliang was ordered to see a husband and wife bound for northern Jiangsu onto their boat at the Wusong estuary, and it was the evening of the next day before he got home. But Xiufen was not there. That had never happened before. Every day Xiufen sat by the cutting-board at the window, embroidering pillowcases; when she had finished thirty pairs she wrapped them in a bedsheet and carried them to the Baishunlai outfitter's on Seymour Road. In Zhongliang's eyes, Shanghai for this woman came down to the vegetable market and the outfitter's on Seymour Road.

Zhongliang lay awake in bed until past midnight before he heard the door. He got up and switched on the light. Xiufen stood in the dim glow in an old cheongsam he had never seen, her face thickly painted, like a streetwalker with her head bowed at the roadside. A flowered cloth handbag was tucked under her arm.

Zhongliang said nothing at all, only looked at her. Xiufen said nothing either; she lowered her head, went into the kitchen, and was a long time washing before she came out. Not once did she glance at Zhongliang. She got into bed as though asleep.
The next day Xiufen opened her eyes to find Zhongliang sitting at the head of the bed. He had plainly not slept the whole night; just now he was clumsily fitting together a pistol he had taken apart.

“A Colt automatic? Quality goods, this.” Not until he had the gun assembled and a round chambered did Zhongliang look at Xiufen and say, “You hid it well. I turned the whole kitchen over before I found it.”
Xiufen snatched the gun back and went down into the kitchen. Her voice came out from there: “You'll be late.”
Zhongliang sat on the edge of the bed without moving, his head bowed, looking at his own two thighs.
“Get to work.” Xiufen came out of the kitchen, took up the yellow cap and put it in his hand.
Zhongliang looked up at her. “You might at least say something.”
“There's nothing to say.” Xiufen sighed, paused, and said, “Go out and buy a paper and you'll know.”

The most conspicuous headline in the paper was a shooting the night before: the dead man a tea merchant come up to Shanghai from the Jiangsu–Anhui border, the place the doorway of a wine-house on Fourth Avenue.
Zhongliang flung the paper down in front of Zhou San and looked him in the eye. Zhou San held the paper a good while, then raised his head. “What tea merchant?” Zhou San smiled. “Rubbish.”
“Who is she, really?”
“A traitor.” Zhou San pointed at the photograph in the paper. “Does that even need saying?”
“I'm talking about Xiufen.” Zhongliang swept the paper to the floor. “You're the one who brought her into my home.”
Zhou San smiled again. “She's your woman.”
Zhongliang sat down slowly, fixed his eyes on him, and held up four fingers. “Four years. I've followed you four years. Can't you tell me one true word?”
But Zhou San stood up, his face set. “Then you ought to understand. What you're not meant to know, I won't say a word of.”

But Zhongliang came to know it all the same, that very evening after supper. Xiufen did not busy herself clearing the bowls and chopsticks as she always did; she sat at one end of the table, looking at Zhongliang, and told him slowly that she was a member of the anti-Japanese assassination squad. The night before, she and her comrades had spent three bullets to remove a turncoat of the New Fourth Army in northern Jiangsu, a man first bought by the Chongqing side who now meant to go over to Nanjing. He had died in the street like a dog. “That,” Xiufen said, her face without expression, “is how a traitor ends.”
Zhongliang said not a word; he only looked at the two hands Xiufen had laid on the table.

It was a strange night. For the first time in two years Xiufen pressed herself to him in bed and reached out to stroke him. But Zhongliang gave no response at all; his hands stayed pillowed behind his head, and he stared, unmoving, at the pitch-black ceiling above the bed.
Xiufen sighed, drew back her hand, and with it drew back her body. In the dark she said, “I shouldn't have let you know any of this. I've broken the rules of the organization.”
It was a long while before Zhongliang spoke. “I was thinking — will there come a day when you fire on me?”
“Yes.” Xiufen said it without hesitation. “If you sell out the organization.”

Late one night that autumn, Zhou San put on a felt cap, left the lodge at the post office, and never came back. The rumors came thick after. Some said he had struck it rich on a lottery ticket and gone home to his village to be a landlord. Others said he had run off with some little whore, and had cleaned out his old flame's valuables before he left. But most of the postmen reckoned he was dead — dead in some prostitute's bed, and dumped into the Huangpu under cover of night. Such things happened often enough on the Shanghai waterfront. Zhongliang, though, thought all at once of his father's cruel death. He gave no thought to the letters he was meant to deliver but pedaled straight home, and the moment he was through the door he said to Xiufen, “We have to go. Stay a few days at your old home.”

Xiufen stopped her needlework and asked what had happened. Zhongliang said Zhou San had disappeared. That said, he opened the cupboard and began to pack up the clothes of them both. Xiufen sat where she was and did not move. “Without an order,” she said, “you can go nowhere.”
“And if he's been arrested?”

“Arrest is not the same as turning traitor. If he had turned, you'd be past leaving already.” As she spoke Xiufen rose and, one piece at a time, put back into the cupboard the clothes Zhongliang had taken out; then she turned to him. “If he really has been arrested, he'll have left you a signal.”
“And if there was no time to leave one?”
Xiufen got up, took him by one arm, and drew him all the way to the door. “Behave as though nothing has happened,” she said. “Go on delivering your letters.”
Zhongliang looked at her face. There were many times when her eyes made him feel she was not really a woman at all.

Three days later, at dusk, Mr. Pan sent for Zhongliang in a hotel room. When they met, Mr. Pan did not mention Zhou San; instead he drew out a news digest and had him read it first. The items in it were all foreign: the British, American, and Dutch colonial governments had all declared an embargo on the shipment of strategic materials to Japan — steel and oil above all; and President Roosevelt had ordered the American fleet into Pearl Harbor. Mr. Pan waited patiently until Zhongliang had read every word, and then said, “From now on you take over Old Zhou's work. Your code name is Catfish.”
As he spoke, he set a silver crucifix down in front of Zhongliang.

Zhongliang said nothing; he picked up the crucifix and studied it closely. He had seen such a crucifix in his father's lifetime, hung about his neck. Zhongliang looked up at Mr. Pan. “What became of Old Zhou?”
“This is the organization's trust in you.” Mr. Pan took one of Zhongliang's hands and said, in earnest, “All these years I've been watching you. I believe you're equal to it.”
Still Zhongliang pressed. “He's dead?”

Only then did Mr. Pan nod. He walked to the window, lifted a corner of the curtain, and gazed out at the street where the evening lamps were coming on. Zhou San had drowned in the Huangpu, he said; the body had been found by a fisherman yesterday morning, and since it was dragged up it had lain in the mortuary of the Leji Tang benevolent hall, but they could not go to claim it yet. Mr. Pan turned back to him. “Do you believe he drowned in the Huangpu?”
Zhongliang lowered his head and thought once more of his father. “Then I'll go and see to his body,” he said.
Mr. Pan shook his head. “No.”
“Why?”
“Your position does not allow it.”
“I'm only a postman.”
“Not anymore.” Mr. Pan said, “You are now the liaison between us and the Far East intelligence service.”

Even so, Zhongliang still rode his bicycle through the lanes and streets every day, deciphering the intelligence he gathered, sorting it, then delivering it on to the various contact points that needed it. All of this had once been Zhou San's work. Zhongliang grew busier; the day was not long enough, and often he had to go out again at night, just as his father once had. Intelligence matters more than a life, because there are times it can save many more lives. These were the words Mr. Pan had spoken, holding his hand at parting. Mr. Pan had said too: “You must make friends with the priest at St. Thérèse's Church. He is the Far East station's contact man in Shanghai — but you must know what to say and what not to say.”

Zhongliang understood at last how his father had come to be a churchgoer. In the confessional at St. Thérèse's Church he passed the silver crucifix in, and it was a long time before he heard Father Brown say, “God bless you, my child.”

One day, on his way out of the confessional, Zhongliang said to Father Brown, “Please help me gather intelligence on the 88th Division of the National Revolutionary Army.” Father Brown said, “That sort of intelligence is not within our exchange.”
“Can't you do me this one favor?” Zhongliang said. “I want to know.”

This was what Su Lina had written in secret ink inside a letter submitted as a manuscript; she had asked Zhongliang to do her the favor. Su Lina had become like a literary bluestocking now, shutting herself away each day in Qin Zhaokuan's apartment, the very picture of the singsong girl who knows nothing of a fallen nation's grief. She wrote poems and essays, sealed them into envelopes, and dropped them in the postbox. Before these manuscripts went on to the newspaper offices, they came first into the postman's hands. Zhongliang deciphered the intelligence Su Lina had drawn from Qin Zhaokuan, and at the same time read the desolate voice of a woman's heart.

Su Lina would sometimes take Qin Zhaokuan's arm and go with him to his various social engagements. The place they went most often was No. 76 on Jessfield Road; now and then they would drink sake at the Japanese Naval Club in Hongkou. Qin Zhaokuan had said that the smell of sake always brought back the dozen-odd years he had spent in Japan. Once, when he had drunk too much of it, he held Su Lina and said in her ear, “You know? The first time I saw you was at your wedding. I kept asking myself then — why am I not the groom?”

Qin Zhaokuan was a gentle, deeply devoted man. Su Lina could see he had already come to think of himself as her husband. Except when he went to Nanjing on business, he returned to her bed almost every night.

It was in bed that Qin Zhaokuan suddenly spoke of Kagoshima. He had come back from a banquet at Nakamura Nobuo's residence, and the moment he lay down he said that Nakamura, it turned out, had a son, a pilot in the navy; for over a month now they had all been drilling in bombing runs at Kagoshima. Qin Zhaokuan said he had no idea what these Japanese meant to bomb next. Su Lina asked idly what sort of place Kagoshima was. Qin Zhaokuan said it was a fine place, at the very southern tip of Japan. That said, he rolled over on top of Su Lina and added, “If you marry me, we'll honeymoon in Kagoshima.”
Su Lina lowered her eyes. “If I ever marry again,” she said, “I mean to honeymoon in London.”
“London these days is worse off than Shanghai,” Qin Zhaokuan said. “It's nearly bombed to rubble.”

The next day Su Lina wrote this too in secret ink on a manuscript and dropped it in the postbox. Another day passed, and when Zhongliang was ordered to carry the news to Father Brown, the priest led him for the first time up to the bedroom on the floor above.

Father Brown's bedroom was like a study. From a great heap of travel maps he drew one out, pointed, and said, “This is Kagoshima. I have been there.” Then, one by one, he pulled out travel maps of Hong Kong, Singapore, the Philippines, and Indonesia, saying with a smile that collecting these things had taken up the better part of his life. When he had compared all the maps, he straightened up and said to Zhongliang, “Which would you say it most resembles?”
Zhongliang handed him a Traffic Map of the United States he had been leafing through for some while, pointed to one of its pages, and said, “This one's very like it.”
Father Brown glanced at it, and his eyes went suddenly rigid. He said, in English, “This is Honolulu, is America.”
